html:
The Dravidians are the peoples of South Asia who speak Dravidian languages, among them Telugu, Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam. The map uses the name from 3000 to 700 BCE for the peoples of the south, and for a time for much of the subcontinent.

Their early history is debated. Many scholars think a form of Proto-Dravidian may have been spoken in the Indus Valley civilisation, though its script is unread and this is not proven. Brahui, a Dravidian language still spoken in Pakistan's Baluchistan, hints that Dravidian speech once reached far into the north-west. In the south, Neolithic herders and farmers kept cattle and grew millets from about 3000 BCE.

The shrinking of the Dravidian area on the map after 1500 BCE reflects the arrival of Indo-Aryan speakers, the Vedic Aryans, in the north. Dravidian languages lent words and sounds to Sanskrit. In the south the megalith builders came next, and from them grew the Tamil kingdoms of the Cheras, Cholas and Pandyas and the poems of Sangam literature. Today around 250 million people speak Dravidian languages.
